query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Brittle behavior in an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy emerges when service‐load (mechanical and thermal) activation induces nanoscale chemical ordering at grain boundaries that locally precipitates brittle intermetallic phases. This stress-assisted ordering mechanism differs from conventional alloy embrittlement, which primarily depends on equilibrium grain-boundary segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A uniform, single-phase compositionally complex (high-entropy) alloy without detectable second phases or grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject alloy specimens to controlled cyclic mechanical loading combined with moderate temperature variations designed to simulate service conditions, particularly those known to induce low-temperature embrittlement or stress-driven structural evolution.
generation.conditions: Loading and temperature regimes relevant for demanding engineering service, e.g., low to moderate testing temperatures and cyclic (or sustained) mechanical stress levels that are high enough to activate local atomic ordering without inducing gross microstructural changes like grain coarsening.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale chemically ordered regions at or near grain boundaries that subsequently act as nucleation sites for brittle intermetallic phase formation.
generation.mechanism: Under cyclic mechanical stresses and moderate temperature fluctuations, local stresses at grain boundaries drive subtle segregation of specific elements. This triggers nanoscale chemical ordering that lowers the local energy barrier for forming brittle intermetallic phases. The newly formed phases at the boundaries reduce the alloy's ability to absorb energy, leading to embrittlement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial single-phase baseline, the alloy will exhibit a measurable decrease in toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness values) coupled with the appearance of nanoscale ordered regions and minute intermetallic precipitates concentrated at grain boundaries, as detected by high-resolution microscopy.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, uniformly single-phase high-entropy alloy with high toughness and ductility as initially measured.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under service-like conditions where temperatures and cyclic stresses are moderate. At significantly higher stresses or temperatures that may induce global microstructural changes (like widespread grain coarsening), different degradation mechanisms might dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise stress or temperature thresholds required to trigger the local chemical ordering are not fully established, and the sensitivity of different high-entropy alloy compositions to this mechanism requires further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of the single-phase high-entropy alloy and, for controlled comparison, specimens of a conventional alloy known to embrittle via grain-boundary segregation under similar conditions. Subject both sets to identical cyclic loading and moderate temperature cycles. Use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to monitor for the formation of nanoscale ordered regions and intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries before and after loading.
measurements: Fracture toughness and ductility before and after the intervention
Microstructural analysis via TEM and APT focusing on grain boundaries
Elemental mapping to detect local chemical ordering of specific constituents
Comparison of the extent of any intermetallic phase formation between the two alloy types
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, after exposure to the simulated service conditions, the high-entropy alloy does not show any detectable nanoscale ordered regions or intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries and maintains its initial level of toughness; or if similar microstructural changes are observed in both the high-entropy and conventional alloys such that the mechanism cannot be distinguished as specific to high-entropy alloys.
